title: Kirtan at home
hookLine: many families sing a shabad in the evening or before sleep

lines: THE TV IN THE NEXT ROOM.
A SHABAD AS THE LIGHTS GO OFF.
cards: Every home has its evening sounds. The TV murmuring in another room. A dishwasher.
Someone scrolling, someone arguing about homework, a phone buzzing on the counter long after anyone should answer it. In many Punjabi homes, the evening has another sound.
A grandmother on the edge of her bed, singing a shabad softly as the lights go off. A father with a small harmonium on the living room rug, a child next to him, both a little out of tune.
Or a phone on the nightstand playing a hymn quietly while someone falls asleep. The gurdwara has its own evening programs. The home has every night.

teach.b: For nine days you've been learning kirtan. Today it comes home. Sikh daily life has an evening shape.
The Sikh code of conduct sets Rehras Sahib, the evening prayer, for sunset.
And last thing at night, before sleep, comes Kirtan Sohila, a short set of five shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib. Its very name has kirtan in it: sohila is a song of praise, a song of joy.
It's the same prayer sung when the Granth is put to rest in the gurdwara at night, and at the end of a Sikh funeral. So the day, the scripture and a life all close with it.
Remember the line from day ninety-six, that in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One? It comes from Kirtan Sohila. Some Sikh children grow up falling asleep to it.

Not every family recites the whole thing aloud together every night. They might sing one shabad after dinner, or play a recording as the house goes quiet, or a parent might sing one line at a bedside.

It doesn't need to be polished; it's not a concert. The Gurus lived as householders, and their hymns were sung in kitchens and courtyards long before any grand building. And consider what it does to a home.

teach.h: THE LAST SOUND OF THE DAY.
teach.b: The last sound of the day isn't the news, or a notification, or an argument.
It's a hymn, and the rooms fill up with it. Over years, some children remember it the way others remember a lullaby. This closes the kirtan days.

how: Many Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and families often sing or play a shabad at home in the evening.

o: five short shabads sung before sleep
a festival of hymns held once a year
the morning prayer said at sunrise

games.q: what's inside the evening — tap the pairs.

put to rest with Kirtan Sohila

games.q: it's bedtime. the phone is still buzzing and the house is noisy. you want to try kirtan at home. what's the smallest step?
o: wait until you can recite Kirtan Sohila perfectly.
put the phone face down and sing one line softly.
only do it on weekends at the gurdwara.
games.why: one line at the bedside is kirtan at home. Kirtan Sohila closes the Sikh day, and a single line can too.

practice: Picture your room at bedtime, the light low, the phone face down on the nightstand, and sing your one line from two days ago very softly, the way you'd sing to a child who's nearly asleep, or sing Waheguru a few times.
Let the sound fill the space around you, then fade, and stay in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan Sohila. The short set of five shabads sung before sleep, and, with Rehras at sunset, part of how the Word lives in ordinary houses.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: a song of praise and joy, as in Kirtan Sohila.
